text.p: These are the leading stories in the Turkish press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan faces his most difficult week yet. Today he must approve the sackings of Islamist officers from the strictly secularist army and on Saturday he will have to account for himself before a top military-dominated council, which has demanded he crack down on Islamist zeal.
- A commission will meet tomorrow to raise the minimum wage, which has fallen to $85 a month.
- Afghan General Abdul Rashid Dostum has sought refuge in Turkey after losing control to pro-Islamist forces in northern Afghanistan.
- Turkish, Greek, Greek and Turkish Cypriot businessmen have agreed in principle that free trade should be conducted between the two communities of divided Cyprus.
- Turkish troops have crushed separatist rebel Kurds in northern Iraq with a cross-border operation into the Kurdish-controlled region.
- Diyarbakir, the main town in southeast Turkey, has potential to become the textile centre of the Middle East.
- Prime Minister Erbakan is planning to try and rule with a minority government if his conservative allies desert him under secularist pressure.
- The Treasury is going to ask banks for help in repaying some of its debts.

- The opposition conservative Motherland Party has been split over resignations from Erbakan's conservative allies. While one wing of Motherland is worried that the resignations are damaging the right-wing, others are pleased and want to channel the former government MPs into their own party.
- Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller is planning to resign from government after Erbakan refused to hand over the premiership.
- Secularists staged protest in Istanbul in support of democracy, which they say has been damaged by the Islamist-conservative government.
